curriculum.lesson_evidence: Disagreements are normal when people have different ideas. A fair way to solve one is: stop and calm down, say what happened using an 'I' statement, listen to the other person, think of options together and choose one that is fair to everyone. If the problem is too big, or someone is unsafe or being hurt, ask a trusted adult for help. Hurting people or things never solves a disagreement.

lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Two friends disagree about who owns a drawing they made together. Write the first two steps of a fair solution, using an 'I' statement.

FEEDBACK
Step 1: stop and breathe. Step 2: 'I feel worried because I put a lot of work into the drawing and I would like us to decide together.' This begins calmly and shares the problem without blame.

WATCH FOR
Thinking that the loudest person, or the winner of an argument, has solved it. A good solution is one that both people can accept.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Write a five-step disagreement plan as a flowchart and use it on two made-up problems (a game rule and a shared item). For each, write a fair solution and name when an adult must help.

Write a short reflection naming one choice you changed and why. Any movement is optional, adult-supervised and can be done in a gentler way or described instead.

teach_steps.explain:
Disagreements are normal when people have different ideas. A fair way to solve one is: stop and calm down, say what happened using an 'I' statement, listen to the other person, think of options together and choose one that is fair to everyone. WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner make safe, healthy and respectful choices using clear cues and reasons, rather than guessing or copying others. Every choice keeps bodies safe and includes everyone.

Step 3: listen ('I only had one go'). Step 4: options (take turns, 10 swings each, ask a teacher). Step 5: choose 10 swings each, then swap. They say thank you.
teaching.rule: Use an intentionally unsafe or unhelpful choice as a comparison. Name the specific PDHPE error, then show the safer or more respectful choice.
teaching.why: This helps the learner make safe, healthy and respectful choices using clear cues and reasons, rather than guessing or copying others. Every choice keeps bodies safe and includes everyone.

teaching.feedback: The new situation should use the same PDHPE idea as the example, but happen in a different place or with different people.
teaching.fix: Change the choice or strategy, not just the wording.
teaching.guided_attempt: Describe or practise one fresh situation that uses the same skill and write a short reason for your choice.
teaching.misconception: Repeating the worked example cannot show transfer to a new situation.
teaching.model: Disagreements are normal when people have different ideas. A fair way to solve one is: stop and calm down, say what happened using an 'I' statement, listen to the other person, think of options together and choose one that is fair to everyone. If the problem is too big, or someone is unsafe or being hurt, ask a trusted adult for help. Hurting people or things never solves a disagreement. Now choose a different situation to show you can transfer the idea.
teaching.rule: Use the same PDHPE idea in a new place, game or situation, not a copy of the example. Review safety, fairness and inclusion.
